mainTopic: When the רבנן penalize accidental sins: רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה on שביעית, שבת and other cases
overview: Just before this amud, רבי מאיר taught that a tree planted on שבת by accident may stay, but a tree planted during שביעית must be uprooted even if it was an accident. He gives two reasons. First, people count years from שביעית but not days from שבת. Second, people were suspected of breaking שביעית but not שבת. The גמרא explains that the second reason is needed because sometimes the exact planting day, even a שבת, does matter. It then explains why רבי יהודה did not penalize for שביעית: in his area people already took it very seriously, as a story about an insult shows. Next, a ברייתא about paying back תרומה with impure חולין seems to show that רבי מאיר does not penalize accidental sinners. The גמרא answers that a person who slips up while trying to do a good act, like paying back, atoning, tithing or purifying utensils, is never penalized. Finally, the גמרא begins a contradiction between two statements of רבי יהודה about rabbinic laws, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: No one counts from שבת
steps.stepSummary: This line finishes רבי מאיר's first reason. People count years for שביעית, but they do not count from a שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And people do not count from שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes the first reason רבי מאיר gave for being strict about שביעית but lenient about שבת. People count from a שביעית year, but they do not count from a שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a tree was planted during שביעית, people keep track of the year, so the tree stays a public reminder of a sin and must be uprooted. Nobody remembers which day of the week a tree was planted. So a tree planted on שבת by accident reminds no one of anything, and it may stay.

keyTerms.meaning: they count (keep track of time from that point)
שבתות, the weekly days of rest
the seventh year (שמיטה), when the land must rest

phrases.english: And they do not count from Shabbatot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the first reason that began just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Planting on שבת leaves no lasting reminder, because nobody counts time from a שבת.

steps.title: A second reason: people were suspected about שביעית but not about שבת
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר offers another reason for the difference. ישראל were suspected of breaking שביעית, but not of breaking שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: ישראל were suspected of violating שביעית, but they were not suspected of violating שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר gives a different reason for treating שביעית more strictly than שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People were known to be lax about שביעית, so the רבנן added a penalty even for accidental planting to stop it. People were careful about שבת, so no extra penalty was needed for an accident. This reason works without the 'counting' idea from step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: another explanation; a second reason
they were suspected (of breaking a law)

phrases.english: Another explanation:
The Jewish people were suspected regarding the Sabbatical Year,
but they were not suspected regarding Shabbatot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, independent reason for the same ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The stricter penalty for שביעית exists because people were known to be lax about it, unlike שבת.

steps.title: Why was a second reason needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the words 'another explanation' are adding.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the point of 'another explanation'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי מאיר needed a second reason when he had already given one. This question sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually one good reason is enough. If a second reason is added, the first reason must have had a weak spot. The גמרא wants to find that weak spot.

keyTerms.meaning: what? (Aramaic)

phrases.english: What is meant by "another explanation"?
phrases.notes: The question is really: why give a second reason at all? Wasn't the first one enough?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the second reason in step 2 was added to the first reason in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What weakness in the first reason made the second reason necessary?

steps.title: Sometimes the day of planting, even שבת, does matter
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the first reason can be challenged. Sometimes the thirtieth day before ראש השנה falls on שבת, and then the exact planting day matters for counting the years of ערלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he means: and if you would say that people count from שבת too, since sometimes the thirtieth day falls on שבת. If he planted on that day, it counts for him as a year. If not, it does not count for him as a year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the first reason was not enough. In one case, people would remember that a tree was planted on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For ערלה, a tree planted at least thirty days before ראש השנה gets credit for a whole year. If the thirtieth day is a שבת, planting on that שבת gains a year, and planting one day later does not. So in that case people would remember the planting day, and the 'nobody counts from שבת' reason breaks down.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what he means
and if you would say (bringing up a possible objection)
sometimes
it counts for him as a year

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא is saying people normally count from שבת. This is a special case: the thirtieth day before ראש השנה happens to fall on שבת.

phrases.english: This is what he is saying:
And if you would say Shabbat is also counted,
since sometimes the thirtieth day falls on Shabbat,
phrases.notes: He means the thirtieth day before ראש השנה, the cutoff for a tree to get a whole year's credit.

phrases.english: so that if he planted on that day,
that is when it counts for him as a year,
phrases.notes: This is about counting the three years of ערלה, when a young tree's fruit is forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָא – לָא סָלְקָא לֵיהּ שַׁתָּא,
phrases.english: and if not, it does not count for him as a year,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3 by showing a weak spot in the first reason.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The first reason can be challenged, because when the thirtieth day before ראש השנה falls on שבת, the planting day matters and will be remembered.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first reason from step 1, that nobody counts from שבת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the case of the thirtieth day before ראש השנה, the exact planting day decides whether a year counts, so people would remember a שבת planting.

steps.title: That is why the second reason is needed
steps.stepSummary: Because the first reason can be challenged, רבי מאיר adds the second reason: people were suspected about שביעית but not about שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear another explanation: ישראל were suspected of violating שביעית, but they were not suspected of violating שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer. It repeats the second reason, now showing that it fills the gap left by the first reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'suspicion' reason does not depend on whether anyone remembers the planting day. So even in the thirtieth-day case, the difference between שבת and שביעית still holds. These words repeat step 2, but here they work as the solution to the problem raised in step 4.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר gives two reasons for being stricter about planting in שביעית than on שבת. The second reason, about suspicion, is needed because the first reason, about counting, does not cover a case where the thirtieth day before ראש השנה falls on שבת.

phrases.english: Come and hear another explanation:
phrases.notes: These are the same words as before, but now they are the answer to the question 'Why add a second reason?'

phrases.english: The Jewish people were suspected regarding the Sabbatical Year,
but they were not suspected regarding Shabbatot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer of step 4 by bringing in the second reason as the fix.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The second reason, suspicion about שביעית, is needed because it works even when the planting day on שבת would be remembered.

steps.title: No contradiction between רבי יהודה's two rulings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבי יהודה's two rulings do not clash, because in his area שביעית was treated as very strict.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is no difficulty between one ruling of רבי יהודה and the other ruling of רבי יהודה. In רבי יהודה's area, people treated שביעית as very serious.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an apparent contradiction between two rulings of רבי יהודה. One is about שביעית and the other is about שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה did not give a penalty for an accidental breach of שביעית, even though he did give one in the other case. The reason is local: in his area people already treated שביעית as very strict. A penalty was only needed where people were careless, and in his area there was no such risk.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not a difficulty; there is no contradiction
In his place, in his area
Treated as serious or strict
The seventh year, when the land rests

phrases.english: One ruling of Rabbi Yehuda against the other ruling of Rabbi Yehuda
is not a difficulty
In Rabbi Yehuda's place
the Sabbatical Year was treated as serious by them.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אַדְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After resolving רבי מאיר's position, the גמרא now resolves the parallel contradiction in רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Local circumstances: the strictness people already had in his area made a penalty unnecessary
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יהודה seems to contradict himself, penalizing in one case but not in the case of שביעית
steps.terutzMaskana: In רבי יהודה's area שביעית was already treated strictly, so no penalty was needed

steps.title: A story showing how seriously they took שביעית
steps.stepSummary: A man insulted by being called a convert answered back that at least he does not eat שביעית produce, which shows that eating it was considered shameful.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who said to his friend: 'Convert, son of a convert!' The friend answered him: 'At least I don't eat שביעית produce like you do!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story as proof that people in רבי יהודה's area took שביעית very seriously.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The insulted man struck back by accusing the other man of eating שביעית produce. That only works as a comeback if eating it was seen as something terrible. So the story confirms the claim in the step before.

keyTerms.meaning: A convert (literally, someone who came to live here); used here as an insult
Produce of the seventh year
Like you

phrases.english: For there was a certain man who said to his friend:
Convert, son of a convert!
He said to him:

phrases.aramaic: אֲנָא לָא אָכְלִי פֵּירֵי דִשְׁבִיעִית כְּווֹתָךְ.
phrases.english: I don't eat produce of the Sabbatical Year like you do.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the claim of step 6 that שביעית was treated strictly in רבי יהודה's area.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that people in רבי יהודה's area treated שביעית as very serious
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story in which accusing someone of eating שביעית produce was used as a harsh comeback
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה did not give a penalty for שביעית only because his area was already strict about it, as the story of the insult proves.

steps.title: A ברייתא about paying back impure תרומה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: if someone ate impure תרומה and paid it back with impure חולין, רבי מאיר says the payment counts only if he did it by accident, and the חכמים say he must pay again with pure produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone ate impure תרומה, he pays back with pure חולין. What if he paid back with impure חולין? סומכוס said in the name of רבי מאיר: if by accident, his payment counts; if on purpose, his payment does not count. The חכמים say: in both cases his payment counts, but he goes back and pays again with pure חולין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a ברייתא about rabbinic penalties. This step sets up a question on רבי מאיר that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר makes a difference between doing something by accident and doing it on purpose. Only on purpose does the impure payment fail to count, which works like a penalty. The חכמים require a second, pure payment in both cases. This ברייתא becomes the base for the challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Impure תרומה, the portion given to the כהן
Ordinary food that is not holy
By accident
On purpose
Payment, repayment

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If one ate impure teruma,
he pays back with pure non-sacred produce.
If he paid with impure non-sacred produce, what is the law?
Sumakhos said in the name of Rabbi Meir:
If by accident, his payment counts as a payment;
if on purpose, his payment does not count as a payment.
And the Sages say:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה תַּשְׁלוּמָיו תַּשְׁלוּמִין,
phrases.english: Whether this case or that case, his payment counts as a payment,
and he goes back and pays again with pure non-sacred produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new discussion about רבי מאיר and rabbinic penalties, using a ברייתא about impure תרומה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: paying back impure תרומה with impure חולין counts if done by accident but not if done on purpose. חכמים: it counts either way, but he must pay again with pure חולין.
steps.confusionAlert: As quoted here, the ברייתא seems to be about impure תרומה repaid with impure חולין. But step 10 shows that words are missing: impure תרומה can be repaid with anything, and the argument is really about pure תרומה.

steps.title: Why shouldn't an on-purpose impure payment count?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי מאיר: the כהן actually gains, because impure חולין can at least be eaten while he is impure, and impure תרומה could never be eaten.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we discussed this: if he did it on purpose, why does his payment not count? He deserves a blessing! He ate from the כהן something that was not fit for him even in his days of impurity, and he pays him back with something that is fit for him in his days of impurity!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי מאיר's ruling that an on-purpose payment with impure חולין does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן may never eat impure תרומה, so what was eaten was useless to him. Impure חולין, however, can be eaten by the כהן when he himself is impure. So the payment is worth more to the כהן than what was taken, and rejecting it seems unfair.

keyTerms.meaning: And we discussed it; introduces an earlier question on the source
May blessing come upon him; meaning he deserves praise, not a penalty
During the days when he (the כהן) is impure
Fit, usable

phrases.english: And we discussed it:
If on purpose, why does his payment not count as a payment?
May blessing come upon him!
For he ate from him something
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the כהן who owned the תרומה.

phrases.english: that is not fit for him even in his days of impurity,
and he pays him back with something
that is fit for him in his days of impurity!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָוֵינַן בַּהּ: בְּמֵזִיד אַמַּאי אֵין תַּשְׁלוּמָיו תַּשְׁלוּמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי מאיר's ruling in the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's ruling that an on-purpose payment with impure חולין does not count
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Impure תרומה is useless to the כהן, while impure חולין can be eaten by him when he is impure. So the payment is an improvement and should surely count.

steps.title: The ברייתא is missing words: the argument is only about pure תרומה
steps.stepSummary: רבא (or an unnamed voice) answers the challenge by reading missing words into the ברייתא. Impure תרומה can be repaid with anything. The argument between רבי מאיר and the חכמים is only about someone who ate pure תרומה and repaid with impure חולין.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said, and some say this was said without a name: The ברייתא is missing words, and this is what it teaches: If someone ate impure תרומה, he can pay back with anything. If he ate pure תרומה, he pays back with pure חולין. If he paid back with impure חולין, what is the law? סומכוס says in the name of רבי מאיר: If he did it by accident, his payment counts. If he did it on purpose, his payment does not count. And the חכמים say: Either way his payment counts, but he must go back and pay again with pure חולין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 9 by saying the ברייתא is missing some words. Once they are filled in, the ברייתא is talking about pure תרומה, not impure תרומה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge was that repaying impure תרומה with impure חולין actually helps the כהן, so why should it ever fail? The answer is that impure תרומה really can be repaid with anything. The argument between רבי מאיר and the חכמים is only about pure תרומה, where the כהן lost food he could eat while pure and got back food that is impure.

keyTerms.meaning: The text is missing words, and we fill them in to read it correctly
Anything at all, even impure produce
A payment, here the payment to the כהן for תרומה that was eaten
By accident, without knowing
On purpose, knowing it was wrong

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. Eating IMPURE תרומה can be repaid with anything, and nobody argues about it. The argument is only about eating PURE תרומה and repaying with impure חולין.

phrases.english: And Rava said, and some say it was said without a name:
phrases.notes: Literally "some say it was just so," meaning nobody's name is attached to this answer.

phrases.english: It is missing words, and this is what it teaches:

phrases.aramaic: אָכַל תְּרוּמָה טְמֵאָה – מְשַׁלֵּם כָּל דְּהוּ.
phrases.english: If he ate impure terumah, he pays back with anything.

phrases.aramaic: אָכַל תְּרוּמָה טְהוֹרָה – מְשַׁלֵּם חוּלִּין טְהוֹרִים.
phrases.english: If he ate pure terumah, he pays back with pure chullin.
If he paid back with impure chullin, what is the law?
Sumchus says in the name of Rabbi Meir:
If by accident, his payment counts as a payment,
if on purpose, his payment does not count as a payment.

phrases.aramaic: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה –
phrases.english: And the Sages say: both this case and that case,
his payment counts as a payment,
and he goes back and pays again with pure chullin.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 9 by reading missing words into the ברייתא of Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: חסורי מחסרא, filling in missing words so the ברייתא is about pure תרומה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was about impure תרומה repaid with impure חולין, which actually helps the כהן.
steps.terutzMaskana: Impure תרומה is repaid with anything. The argument is only about pure תרומה repaid with impure חולין, where the כהן does lose.

steps.title: Does this show רבי מאיר does not penalize accidental sinners?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא says the argument here is whether we penalize an accidental sinner because of someone who sins on purpose. That means רבי מאיר does not penalize the accidental sinner, which seems to clash with the earlier idea that he does.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב אחא the son of רב איקא said: Here, what they argue about is whether the חכמים penalized someone who acted by accident because of someone who acted on purpose. (רבי מאיר holds they did not penalize the accidental one because of the deliberate one, and the חכמים say they did penalize him.)
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא explains what the argument in the ברייתא is really about. This explanation turns into a challenge, because it puts רבי מאיר on the side of NOT penalizing someone who acted by accident.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא held that רבי מאיר penalizes even accidental breaking of a rabbinic law. Here he lets the accidental payer off and only penalizes the one who did it on purpose. So the two statements about רבי מאיר seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: They (the חכמים) imposed a penalty, a fine set by the Rabbis
Because of, so that people will not come to the other case
There is a difference between them, this is what they argue about

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether the רבנן penalize an accident because of people who do it on purpose is a key idea all through this סוגיא, and it decides how we understand רבי מאיר's whole approach.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא:
phrases.english: And Rav Acha, son of Rav Ika, said:
Here, about whether they penalized the accidental one because of the deliberate one,
is what they argue about

phrases.aramaic: (דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר סָבַר: לֹא קָנְסוּ שׁוֹגֵג אַטּוּ מֵזִיד,
phrases.english: (that Rabbi Meir holds: they did not penalize the accidental one because of the deliberate one,
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets.

phrases.english: and the Sages say: they did penalize)!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּקָנְסוּ שׁוֹגֵג אַטּוּ מֵזִיד אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the corrected ברייתא from Step 10 and uses it to raise a contradiction about רבי מאיר.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier view that רבי מאיר penalizes even accidental breaking of a rabbinic law
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the ברייתא רבי מאיר accepts an accidental payment and only rejects a deliberate one, so he does not penalize the accidental case.

steps.title: This case is different because the man was trying to pay
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison. In the payment case the man was trying to do the right thing by paying the כהן, so it makes no sense to penalize him.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them?! There, the man is trying to pay. Should we get up and penalize him?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 11 by showing that the payment case is special.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר does penalize accidents in general. But here the man made his mistake while trying to pay back what he owed, which is a good thing to do. Fining someone in the middle of doing the right thing makes no sense, so the payment case is an exception and not a contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare? The cases are not alike
He intends, he is trying to
Should we get up and penalize him? (said as a question that expects "no")

phrases.english: How can you compare?!
There, the man is trying to pay,
should we get up and penalize him?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 11 by separating the payment case from other cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: no penalty when the mistake came while doing a good act
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר's ruling about payment shows he never penalizes accidental sinners.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר penalizes accidents in general, but not here, because the man was trying to pay the כהן.

steps.title: Test case: impure blood sprinkled on the מזבח
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: if blood of a קרבן became impure and the כהן sprinkled it anyway, it counts if he did it by accident but not if he did it on purpose. This seems to show that this תנא does not penalize the accidental case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If blood became impure and the כהן sprinkled it, if he did it by accident the קרבן is accepted, and if he did it on purpose the קרבן is not accepted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to test whether a rabbinic penalty is given for an accident. This sets up the next part of the discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sprinkling impure blood is forbidden only by the Rabbis, yet the ברייתא lets the accidental case count and only punishes the deliberate one. That looks like a source where the accidental sinner is NOT penalized because of the deliberate one, so it presses again on the view of רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: He sprinkled it on the מזבח
It was accepted, the קרבן worked and brought atonement

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Blood that became impure, and he sprinkled it;
if by accident, it is accepted,
if on purpose, it is not accepted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new source to test the question from Steps 11-12, whether an accidental sinner is penalized because of a deliberate one.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the Rabbis penalize an accidental breaking of a rabbinic law because of people who break it on purpose
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about impure blood sprinkled on the מזבח: by accident it is accepted, on purpose it is not.

steps.title: The blood case is different because the person wanted to atone
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר pushes away the proof from the impure blood. The person sprinkling was trying to get atonement, so we would never penalize him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר could answer you: How can you compare? There the person is trying to get atonement. Should we get up and penalize him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from the last step. It says רבי מאיר would answer that the blood case is special.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the blood case, the person was busy with a מצוה: he was trying to bring a קרבן and get כפרה. Even רבי מאיר agrees we don't penalize someone like that. So the case proves nothing about ordinary accidental sinners.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare? (the cases are not alike)
the man, the person
to atone, to get atonement
we should penalize him (from קְנָס, a penalty)

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir could say to you:
How can you compare?!
There, the man is trying to get atonement,
phrases.notes: "There" means the case of the impure blood that was sprinkled.

phrases.english: should we get up and penalize him?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ רַבִּי מֵאִיר: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes away the proof brought in step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the blood case to show that רבי מאיר never penalizes the accidental sinner.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The blood case involves someone trying to do a מצוה (atonement), and a case like that is different.

steps.title: A proof from someone who tithes on שבת
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new source. Someone who tithed on שבת by accident may eat the food. If he did it on purpose, he may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Someone who tithes on שבת: if by accident, he may eat; if on purpose, he may not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a second proof that we don't penalize the accidental sinner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tithing on שבת is not allowed, yet the person who did it by accident may still eat his food. Only the one who did it on purpose loses out. So this source seems to treat the two people differently and not penalize the accidental one.

keyTerms.meaning: one who tithes (separates מעשר from produce)
by accident, unintentionally
on purpose, intentionally

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who tithes on Shabbat:
if by accident, he may eat it,
if on purpose, he may not eat it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was pushed away, a new proof is brought.
steps.raayaObject: That we do not penalize an accidental sinner because of an intentional one.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה about tithing on שבת.

steps.title: The tithing case is different because the person wanted to fix his food
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed away. The person was trying to make his food fit to eat, so we don't penalize him.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare? There the man is trying to fix the food. Should we get up and penalize him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the tithing proof with the same kind of answer it used before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tithing is a good act: it makes the food permitted. Someone who does a good act and slips up is not penalized. That says nothing about a regular accidental sinner.

keyTerms.meaning: to fix, to make proper (here: to make the food fit to eat)

phrases.english: How can you compare?!
There, the man is trying to fix the food,
should we get up and penalize him?!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא?! הָתָם – גַּבְרָא לְתַקּוֹנֵי קָא מִיכַּוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes away the tithing proof from step 15.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the tithing case as a proof.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The person was trying to do something good (fix the food), so the case is special.

steps.title: A proof from someone who immerses utensils on שבת
steps.stepSummary: A third source: someone who immersed utensils on שבת by accident may use them. If he did it on purpose, he may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Someone who immerses utensils on שבת: if by accident, he may use them; if on purpose, he may not use them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third proof that we don't penalize the accidental sinner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again the accidental one is allowed to benefit, and only the one who did it on purpose is penalized. This seems to show we don't penalize the accidental sinner because of the intentional one.

keyTerms.meaning: one who immerses (in a מקוה)
utensils, vessels
he may use

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who immerses utensils on Shabbat:
if by accident, he may use them,
if on purpose, he may not use them!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another proof after the tithing proof was pushed away.
steps.raayaObject: That we do not penalize an accidental sinner because of an intentional one.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה about immersing utensils on שבת.

steps.title: The immersion case is different because the person wanted to purify the utensils
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed away. The person was trying to make his utensils pure, so we don't penalize him.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare? There the man is trying to purify the utensils. Should we get up and penalize him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the third proof with the same answer as before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making utensils pure is a good act, just like atoning and tithing. In all three cases the person meant to do something right, so none of them proves anything about ordinary accidental sinners.

keyTerms.meaning: to purify, to make טהור
utensils (Aramaic for כלים)

steps.whatToRemember: All three proofs fall for the same reason. When someone slips up while trying to do a מצוה, we don't penalize him. So these cases can't tell us what רבי מאיר holds about regular accidental sinners.

phrases.english: How can you compare?!

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם – גַּבְרָא לְטַהוֹרֵי מָאנֵי קָא מִיכַּוֵּין,
phrases.english: There, the man is trying to purify the utensils,
should we get up and penalize him?!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא?! הָתָם – גַּבְרָא לְטַהוֹרֵי מָאנֵי קָא מִיכַּוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes away the immersion proof from step 17.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the immersion case as a proof.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The person was trying to do a מצוה (purify utensils), so the case is special.

steps.title: Setting up a contradiction between two statements of רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new topic: two statements of רבי יהודה about rabbinic rules seem to contradict each other. It begins to quote a ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they pointed out a contradiction between one statement of רבי יהודה and another statement of רבי יהודה about rabbinic rules, as it was taught in a ברייתא:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It announces a contradiction within רבי יהודה's own views about rabbinic laws and starts quoting the first source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the discussion was about רבי מאיר. Now the focus moves to רבי יהודה, and the question is about rules that come from the רבנן, not the תורה. The actual sources come next.

keyTerms.meaning: and they pointed out a contradiction (literally: they threw one against the other)
in rabbinic laws (rules made by the חכמים)

phrases.english: And they pointed out a contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yehuda
in rabbinic laws, as it was taught:
phrases.notes: The ברייתא itself is quoted on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the רבי מאיר discussion to a new contradiction about רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's view on penalizing accidental sinners in rabbinic laws.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two of רבי יהודה's statements seem to clash; the sources are about to be quoted.
